questions.stem: A startup raises $2M at a $8M pre-money valuation. The new investor's ownership is:
questions.explanation: Post-money = $8M + $2M = $10M. Ownership = $2M / $10M = 20%. The founders are diluted from 100% to 80%.

questions.stem: If a company has a pre-money valuation of $15M and raises $5M, the post-money valuation is:
questions.explanation: Post-money = pre-money + investment = $15M + $5M = $20M.

questions.stem: Which investor type typically writes the SMALLEST cheques and invests EARLIEST?
choices: Friends, family, and fools (FFF) / pre-seed angels
questions.explanation: FFF/pre-seed angels typically invest under $500k at the earliest stage, often pre-MVP, on the basis of team and idea.

questions.stem: A SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity) is best described as:
choices: Debt with interest and a maturity date.
An agreement that converts to equity at the next priced round, with no interest and no maturity — a Y Combinator innovation now dominant in seed.
questions.explanation: SAFEs replaced convertible notes for many seed rounds because they removed interest and maturity, simplifying the instrument.

questions.stem: A convertible note has a $5M valuation cap and a 20% discount. The next priced round is at $10M pre-money. The note converts at an effective pre-money of:
questions.explanation: Cap gives $5M; discount gives $10M × 80% = $8M. The note converts at the LOWER of the two = $5M. The cap is the binding term here.

questions.stem: Standard VC fund economics are typically:
choices: 2% management fee, 20% carried interest above LP capital
questions.explanation: The classical '2 and 20' structure: 2% annual management fee on committed capital plus 20% of profits above LP returns.

questions.stem: A '1x non-participating' liquidation preference means investors receive:
choices: Nothing on exit until founders are paid.
1x their investment back before common shareholders, then they choose between taking the preference OR converting to common — but not both.
1x their investment plus their pro-rata share of remaining proceeds as common.
questions.explanation: 1x non-participating: investors take the higher of (a) 1x preference or (b) converted-to-common pro-rata share. Standard founder-friendly term.

questions.stem: A '1x PARTICIPATING' liquidation preference is more aggressive because:
choices: Investors get 1x preference AND then participate pro-rata in remaining proceeds — effectively double-dipping.
Investors must invest twice the original amount.
questions.explanation: Participating preference returns the investor's capital first, then lets them share in remaining proceeds as if they were common — a less founder-friendly term.

questions.stem: Founder shares typically vest over what schedule?
choices: All shares vest immediately at funding
questions.explanation: 4-year vesting with a 1-year cliff is the industry standard. Protects against early founder departures destabilising the company.

questions.stem: An option pool of 10-15% reserved for employees, carved out of PRE-money, has what effect on existing shareholders?
choices: No effect — the pool dilutes only future investors.
Dilutes existing shareholders, because the pool is created before the new investor's stake is calculated.
questions.explanation: Pre-money option pool expansion is a standard investor ask. It shifts dilution to existing shareholders and is sometimes called the 'option-pool shuffle'.

questions.stem: Power-law returns in venture capital mean that:
choices: Most VC returns come from a small number of huge winners; many investments return zero or less.
Returns scale with the square root of investment size.
All investments return roughly the same.
questions.explanation: Empirically, ~1-2 deals per fund produce most of the returns. The 'one fund-returner pays for the rest' rule of thumb. Shapes how VCs select and price.

questions.stem: Mailchimp's $12B acquisition with NO venture capital raised is a famous example of:
questions.explanation: Mailchimp self-funded from revenue and exited via acquisition by Intuit. Textbook bootstrapping case study.

questions.stem: Which is NOT typically a Series A criterion?
choices: Founders who can hire a senior team.
questions.explanation: Most Series A companies are not yet profitable. PMF + growth engine + team are the usual criteria.

questions.stem: A startup goes through Seed at $5M post-money (20% sold), then Series A at $20M post-money (25% sold). Approximate cumulative founder ownership (ignoring option pools) is:
questions.explanation: After seed: 80% remaining. After Series A: 80% × (1 - 25%) = 60%. Cumulative dilution multiplies, not adds.

questions.stem: A 'full-ratchet' anti-dilution clause means:
choices: Modest adjustment for a down round.
If a future round prices lower, the prior investor's conversion price is re-set to the new round's price entirely — heavily punitive to founders and common shareholders.
Adjustment only after three down rounds.
questions.explanation: Full-ratchet is the most aggressive anti-dilution: prior investors are made whole as if they had invested at the down-round price. Broad-based weighted average is the founder-friendlier standard.

questions.stem: Which Australian VC firm is known for backing CSIRO-affiliated deep tech?
questions.explanation: Main Sequence is the CSIRO-affiliated deep-tech fund. Blackbird, Square Peg, and AirTree are general-stage Australian VCs.

questions.stem: Pro-rata rights in a term sheet give investors:
choices: The right to veto future rounds.
The right to participate in future rounds to maintain their ownership percentage.
The right to a board seat.
The right to set the valuation.
questions.explanation: Pro-rata rights let existing investors maintain their ownership by participating in subsequent rounds. Highly prized by VCs in winning portfolio companies.

questions.stem: Y Combinator and Techstars are best classified as:
choices: Accelerators that provide small cheques and intensive mentorship to pre-seed startups
questions.explanation: Accelerators provide small standard-terms investments (typically $125k-$500k via SAFE) plus 3-month structured programmes and demo-day exposure.

questions.stem: A startup raises $4M at $16M pre-money. The new investor's ownership is:
questions.explanation: Post-money = $20M. New investor = $4M / $20M = 20%.

questions.stem: Which funding stage is typically the FIRST round with a formal valuation negotiated?
choices: Pre-seed via SAFEs (often capped, no immediate priced valuation)
Priced seed round or Series A — depending on whether the firm uses SAFEs at seed
questions.explanation: If SAFEs are used at seed, the first PRICED round (with a negotiated valuation) is often Series A. Some startups do a priced seed and negotiate valuation earlier.

questions.stem: Drag-along rights on an exit allow:
choices: A minority shareholder to block a sale.
A majority shareholder to force minorities to sell their shares on the same terms in an acquisition.
Investors to claim multiple liquidation preferences.
questions.explanation: Drag-along ensures a deal can close: when the majority approves, minorities are 'dragged' to sell on identical terms. Standard in most term sheets.

questions.stem: Tag-along (co-sale) rights protect:
choices: Minority shareholders by letting them sell pro-rata alongside a majority shareholder who is selling.
questions.explanation: Tag-along is the converse of drag-along: if the majority sells, minorities have the right to join the sale on the same terms.

questions.stem: An 'acqui-hire' is best described as:
choices: An acquisition primarily intended to obtain the target's team, often with minimal return for shareholders.
questions.explanation: Acqui-hires value the people, not the product. Typical outcomes: founder/key engineer retention packages; modest investor return.

questions.stem: A startup raises $10M at $40M pre-money with a 10% option pool TO BE CREATED PRE-MONEY. The new investor's ownership is:
questions.explanation: Post-money = $50M. New investor = $10M / $50M = 20%. The 10% option pool dilutes existing shareholders, not the new investor (it is taken from pre-money).

questions.stem: The classical 'fund-returner' rule of thumb in VC is that:
choices: Every investment must return the entire fund.
A single very-large outcome must be capable of returning the entire fund's committed capital — otherwise the math doesn't work given power-law returns.
All investments are expected to break even.
questions.explanation: Given power-law returns and a typical 20-deal portfolio, each investment must be capable (in success) of returning the whole fund. Shapes VC ticket sizing and target ownership.
